data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinction between genuine reliability gain and mere checklist compliance cannot be established within a single evaluation if the evaluation distribution is drawn from the same population the checklist was calibrated on; distinguishing them requires cross-distribution evidence by necessity.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The single evaluation includes adversarial items constructed to simulate distribution shift internally, making cross-distribution evidence available within one evaluation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The checklist is deductively complete rather than calibrated, so distribution shift does not affect its validity and cross-distribution evidence is unnecessary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The evaluation measures not only accuracy but also intermediate reasoning traces, so compliance and genuine reliability are distinguishable by process evidence even within one distribution.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The evaluation distribution is demonstrably out-of-sample relative to the checklist's calibration set, so the single evaluation already provides cross-distribution evidence.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Within a single evaluation drawn from the calibration distribution, compliance and genuine reliability are observationally equivalent: both produce high accuracy. The distinction becomes empirically meaningful only under distribution shift, where a causally structured checklist survives and a surface-correlational one fails. Since a single evaluation is, by construction, one distribution, it cannot provide the cross-distribution evidence needed. The requested within-evaluation distinction is therefore impossible in principle.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
